Performance: fast paths and slow paths

Source: vignettes/articles/performance.Rmd
performance.Rmd
library(parvenu)

parvenu’s functions are fast without any tuning. A few habits make them faster still, and a few inputs quietly take a slow path. This article collects both. If you are new to parvenu, start with the use case examples, which show what each function is for.

Every timing here comes from one script, bench/performance.R, run on 8 cores. Its output, with the R version and platform, is in bench/performance.out. The numbers are medians, rounded. Run the script to get your own.

Keep repeated values as a factor

A column that repeats a few values, such as a country, a product code, or a status, is faster as a factor. par_match(), %par_in%, and the text functions then work on the levels only, and give each element the result of its level:

country <- factor(c("France", "Peru", "France", "Chad", "Peru"))

country %par_in% c("Peru", "Chad")
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE
par_detect(country, "^P")
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE  TRUE
par_match_term(country, c("an", "er"))
#> [1]  1  2  1 NA  2

The results are the same as for a character vector. With 10 million elements, a factor takes about a tenth of the time:

10 million elements Character Factor
par_match() in 10 million strings, 100 distinct values 79ms 8ms
par_match() in 10 million strings, 100,000 distinct values 107ms 16ms
par_detect(), 100 distinct values 36ms 4ms
par_detect(), 100,000 distinct values 75ms 6ms

Base match() takes 2.3s and 1.6s for the two lookups, factor or not.

So keep such a column as a factor if it already is one, rather than calling as.character() on it first. Converting a character column with par_factor() pays off if you use it more than once. It takes 33ms for 100 distinct values, but 0.56s for 100,000, most of it sorting the levels.

Ask for no more than you need

The threads find the matches, but only R’s own thread can make R strings. So a function that returns positions, counts, or TRUE and FALSE is faster than one that returns strings. For one regex in 100,000 strings:

Function Returns Time
par_detect() logical 2.2ms
par_count() integer 2.9ms
par_locate() integer matrix 3.0ms
par_extract() strings 8.5ms
par_extract_all() list of strings 10ms
par_replace_all() strings 12ms

To filter rows, use par_detect() rather than checking the result of par_extract() for NA. To count words, use par_count() rather than the lengths of par_extract_all().

Many terms: a dictionary, not (?i)

An alternation of literal terms, such as "aspirin|ibuprofen", is fast in par_detect(). With (?i) in front, it is not. par_match_term(ignore_case = TRUE) keeps its speed. For 1,000 terms in 100,000 strings:

Call Time
par_detect(), alternation 51ms
par_detect(), alternation with (?i) 15s
par_match_term() 18ms
par_match_term(ignore_case = TRUE) 18ms

The term functions also keep the automaton of the last terms. Building it for 10,000 terms takes most of the 11ms that a first search of 100 strings needs. A call that repeats the same terms, as on every keystroke in a Shiny app, takes 0.16ms. The same goes for the last regex of par_detect() and its relatives.

One call, not one per chunk

A single call on the whole input beats splitting it across R processes that each call parvenu. Counting a regex in 400,000 strings takes 35ms in one call, and 96ms split across 8 forked workers, since the workers have to start and the results have to come back. Giving each worker one thread doesn’t help: 103ms. Use process pools for R code that parvenu doesn’t cover.

The default is all cores. On a machine you share, set options(parvenu.threads = 4) once, or the RAYON_NUM_THREADS environment variable. Inputs too small to keep that many threads busy use fewer on their own, so there is no need to lower nthreads for them.

Small inputs

The base R family (par_match(), par_duplicated(), par_rank(), and so on) calls base R itself below 10,000 elements. So these functions are within a few microseconds of base there, and safe to use where the size varies. The gain starts right above that size and grows with it:

Elements match() par_match()
1,000 0.01ms 0.02ms
10,000 0.34ms 0.10ms
100,000 18ms 0.7ms

The text functions always run in Rust, since their results differ from base R’s. Below 5,000 strings they use one thread.

Inputs that take a slow path

These give correct results, but at base R’s speed or close to it. None of them warns.

Strings in mixed encodings. par_match(), par_duplicated(), and par_unique() compare strings by where R stores them, which only works if equal strings are stored once. If a vector holds non-ASCII strings both as UTF-8 and as latin1, they leave it to base R. Convert once with enc2utf8():

x <- c("café", iconv("café", "UTF-8", "latin1"))
Encoding(x)
#> [1] "UTF-8"  "latin1"
x <- enc2utf8(x)
Encoding(x)
#> [1] "UTF-8" "UTF-8"

With a single latin1 string among a million, par_match() takes 39ms, more than base match() at 31ms. After enc2utf8(), and including it, it takes 11ms.

Times in a time zone other than UTC. par_as_posixct() reads UTC times directly. In other zones, base R’s code places the local times, on days with a change of clock every one of them. A million times over 54 years take 13ms in UTC and 0.34s in "Europe/Berlin", against 14s and 22s in base. If your times are in UTC, say tz = "UTC" rather than leaving the session’s time zone to decide.

Also pass format if you know it. Without it, the first of tryFormats that reads every string is used, as in base R. A single time that the clock skipped, such as 02:30 on the night it moved from 02:00 to 03:00, is NA in its zone. So it fails every format with a time of day, and the date-only format takes over for the whole vector:

x <- c("2024-03-31 02:30:00", "2024-05-01 12:00:00")
par_as_posixct(x, tz = "Europe/Berlin")
#> [1] "2024-03-31 03:30:00 CEST" "2024-05-01 12:00:00 CEST"
par_as_posixct(x, tz = "Europe/Berlin", format = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
#> [1] "2024-03-31 03:30:00 CEST" "2024-05-01 12:00:00 CEST"

Base as.POSIXct() returns the same. Besides losing the times, trying the formats took 1.1s for a million strings, against 0.29s with format.

Tables of doubles. par_table() and par_factor() turn doubles into their printed values, as base does, which takes seconds for 10 million of them either way. Integers don’t need that. If the values are tenths or cents, tabulate them as whole numbers:

price <- c(1.5, 2.25, 1.5)
par_table(as.integer(round(price * 100)))
#> 
#> 150 225 
#>   2   1

For 10 million values, that is 0.45s against 4.1s.

Sorted values in par_find_interval(). Base findInterval() is already fast when x is sorted, since it doesn’t search from scratch for each value: 25ms for 10 million values into 10,000 breaks, against 28ms here. The gain is for unsorted x, 30ms against 0.91s.

Arguments and classes that go to base R. Each help page says what its function leaves to base. The common ones:

  • incomparables other than FALSE in par_match(), par_duplicated(), and par_unique()
  • classes other than factor, Date, and POSIXct, such as integer64 or difftime
  • ties.method = "random" in par_rank()
  • data frames in par_rowsum()
  • na.rm = FALSE in par_approx()
  • date formats beyond those ?par_as_date lists, and month names in a locale that isn’t English

Joins on several columns

To match on several key columns, pass them to par_match_rows() as they are. Pasting them into one string first costs far more than the match: for two columns of 10 million rows, paste() takes 11s on one thread, and par_match_rows() on the columns themselves 0.07s.

orders <- data.frame(customer = c(1L, 2L, 1L), year = c(2025, 2025, 2026))
targets <- data.frame(customer = c(1L, 1L, 2L), year = c(2026, 2025, 2026))

par_match_rows(orders, targets)
#> [1]  2 NA  1

par_match_all() and par_match_rows_all() return every pair of equal elements. Their result can be far larger than the inputs: 100,000 equal keys on each side make 10 billion pairs. More than 2^31 - 1 pairs are an error, raised before any pair is built.
